Native to eastern and central North American rich woods.

Native to much of northern North America and cool eastern wetlands.

Native to the southwestern U.S. and northern Mexico, including parts of the southern Plains.

Native across much of central and western North America. Use locally sourced seed.

Native to western North American shrublands and dry open slopes, with multiple local varieties.

fieldNotes.butterflyMilkweed: Flat clusters of vivid orange flowers sit above upright, narrow-leaved stems. Bees and butterflies visit the blooms, and monarch caterpillars feed on the leaves.
fieldNotes.njTea: A low, rounded shrub with foamy white flower clusters. Small bees, flies and other insects visit the flowers.
fieldNotes.columbine: Red and yellow bells dangle from airy stems above rounded leaflets. Hummingbirds and long-tongued bees reach into the nectar spurs.
fieldNotes.swampMilkweed: Tall, slender stems carry pink flower clusters and later narrow seedpods. The flowers feed bees and butterflies, and the leaves host monarch caterpillars.
fieldNotes.buttonbush: This spreading shrub bears white, pincushion-like flower balls. Bees and butterflies visit the blooms, and the heads turn into rough brown seed clusters.
fieldNotes.ragwort: Yellow daisies rise above a spreading carpet of rounded leaves. The spring flowers draw small bees and flies.
fieldNotes.mistflower: Fuzzy lavender-blue flower clusters top a colony-forming perennial. The late blooms draw small butterflies and bees.
fieldNotes.bluestem: An upright bunchgrass that turns copper in fall and carries fluffy white seeds. It is wind-pollinated, and its leaves feed some skipper caterpillars.
fieldNotes.bergamot: Lavender flower whorls sit on tall stems with fragrant leaves. Bumblebees, butterflies and hummingbirds visit the tubes.
fieldNotes.geranium: A loose mound of deeply lobed leaves sends up pink to lilac flowers. Spring bees visit for pollen and nectar.
fieldNotes.foxSedge: A clumping sedge with narrow leaves and clusters of brown, bristly seed heads. It is wind-pollinated and adds cover and texture to wet ground.
fieldNotes.prairieClover: Purple flower rings climb slim spikes above fine leaves. Bees work the small flowers, including bees that specialize on prairie clovers.
fieldNotes.bottlebrush: A woodland bunchgrass with long, bristled seed heads that look like bottle brushes. It is wind-pollinated and grows in loose tufts.
fieldNotes.waterleaf: A spreading woodland perennial with lobed leaves, often marked with pale spots when young. Its pale flower clusters are visited by bees.
fieldNotes.whiteIndigo: White pea flowers rise on tall stalks, followed by plump dark pods. Bumblebees visit the flowers, and some butterfly caterpillars use wild indigos as hosts.
fieldNotes.coralHoneysuckle: A twining vine with coral-red trumpets and red berries. The flower tubes are especially inviting to hummingbirds.
fieldNotes.roseMallow: A tall clumping perennial with dinner-plate flowers in white to pink. Bees gather pollen from the prominent central column.
fieldNotes.spottedBeebalm: Pale pink bracts frame tiers of spotted cream flowers. The nectar draws a mix of bees and visiting wasps.
fieldNotes.inkberry: An evergreen shrub with glossy leaves, tiny white blooms and dark berries on pollinated female plants. Bees visit the flowers.
fieldNotes.scarletMallow: Tall leafy stems hold scarlet flowers with five widely separated petals. The blooms are visited by bees and other insects.
fieldNotes.blueGrama: A fine-textured bunchgrass with seed heads shaped like little eyelashes. The flowers are wind-pollinated, and the low foliage works in dry meadow plantings.
fieldNotes.canadaAnemone: Single white flowers rise over deeply divided leaves. Bees and flies visit, and spreading underground stems can form a broad patch.
fieldNotes.poppyMallow: Trailing stems carry magenta cups over lobed leaves. Native bees visit the flowers, including bees associated with the mallow family.
fieldNotes.sideoats: Small oat-like spikelets hang along one side of each arching stem. This wind-pollinated bunchgrass adds movement to dry plantings.
fieldNotes.redbud: Pink pea flowers open directly on bare branches before the heart-shaped leaves expand. Early bees visit the bloom.
fieldNotes.buckwheat: Low mats of leaves send up flat clusters of yellow flowers that age rusty. Small bees, butterflies and flies work the clusters.
fieldNotes.blueColumbine: Airy stems bear blue and white flowers with long nectar spurs. Bumblebees and other long-tongued visitors reach the flowers.
fieldNotes.barberry: This low evergreen spreads under trees and bears yellow flowers followed by blue berries. The spring clusters offer forage to bees.
fieldNotes.hairgrass: Dense tufts of fine leaves carry loose clouds of delicate seed heads. It is wind-pollinated and keeps its airy form as the heads dry.
fieldNotes.desertMarigold: Yellow daisies stand above a low mound of woolly gray leaves. Bees visit the open flowers.
fieldNotes.fairyDuster: A low, fine-leaved shrub with pink sprays of long stamens. Hummingbirds and insects visit the brush-like flowers.
fieldNotes.desertWillow: A small tree with slender leaves, pink trumpet flowers and long pods. Large bees readily visit the open throats.
fieldNotes.clarkia: An upright annual with satiny pink cups. Bees collect pollen from the flowers, and established stands can reseed in open ground.
fieldNotes.woolly: Silver-woolly foliage contrasts with yellow daisies on short stems. The flowers are visited by bees and other small insects.
fieldNotes.oregonGrape: Glossy, prickly evergreen leaves surround yellow spring flowers and blue fruit. Early-season bees visit the flower clusters.
fieldNotes.salal: This spreading evergreen has leathery leaves and hanging clusters of white to pink bells. Bees visit the blossoms before dark berries form.
fieldNotes.camas: Blue-violet stars climb upright spikes over grasslike leaves. Spring bees visit, and the bulb goes dormant after the foliage dies back.
fieldNotes.ninebark: A spreading shrub with white flower clusters and bark that peels in thin strips. Small bees and flies visit the blooms.
fieldNotes.calBuckwheat: A rounded shrub with narrow leaves and creamy flower clusters that dry to rust. Bees, flies and butterflies use the small flowers.
fieldNotes.calFuchsia: Bright red tubes run along low, spreading stems. The late-season flowers are a nectar source for hummingbirds.
fieldNotes.coyoteMint: Aromatic foliage forms a compact mound topped with lavender pom-poms. The clusters draw bees and butterflies.
fieldNotes.calRose: A thorny shrub with open pink flowers and orange-red hips. Bees collect pollen, and the stems can spread into a thicket.
fieldNotes.fireweed: Tall stalks carry pink flowers from the bottom up, then release silky seeds. Bees visit the blooms, and the plant readily spreads on open ground.
fieldNotes.bunchberry: A low, spreading groundcover with a whorl of leaves, four white bracts and a cluster of red berries. Small insects visit the tiny flowers at the center.
fieldNotes.alaskaIris: Sword-shaped leaves form clumps under blue-violet blooms. Bees can enter the broad floral passages to reach the nectar.
fieldNotes.ilima: Papery yellow to orange flowers cover forms ranging from trailing groundcovers to shrubs. Native yellow-faced bees can visit the blooms.
fieldNotes.mossPhlox: Needlelike foliage knits into a low mat covered in spring flowers. Butterflies and other long-tongued insects can reach the nectar in the tubes.
fieldNotes.spicebush: Small yellow spring flowers line bare branches, and pollinated female plants bear red fruit. Small insects visit the blooms, and spicebush swallowtail caterpillars use the leaves.
fieldNotes.blueFlag: Clumps of swordlike leaves send up blue-violet flowers marked with yellow and white. Bees enter beneath the arching flower parts.
fieldNotes.beachPlum: A dense, often suckering shrub with white spring flowers and purple fruit. Bees visit the flowers before the plums form.
fieldNotes.clethra: Fragrant white flower spikes stand above a rounded, often suckering shrub. The summer blooms draw bees, butterflies and other insects.
fieldNotes.sweetfern: Aromatic, deeply cut leaves give this low shrub a fernlike look. Its small catkins are wind-pollinated, and colonies can spread over sandy ground.
fieldNotes.bayberry: An aromatic shrub with leathery leaves and waxy gray berries on female plants. Its inconspicuous flowers are wind-pollinated.
fieldNotes.arcticWillow: A creeping woody mat bears upright catkins above small leathery leaves. Small insects may visit the catkins when they open.
fieldNotes.cottonGrass: A tussock-forming sedge with fluffy white seed tufts on upright stalks. Wind carries the pollen and later disperses the seeds.
fieldNotes.waterSedge: Stiff, narrow leaves and dark upright spikes form dense patches along wet margins. It spreads by rhizomes and is wind-pollinated.
fieldNotes.dryas: A woody mat of scalloped leaves bears cream flowers and feathery seed heads. Flies and other small insects visit the open flowers.
fieldNotes.lyngbye: This rhizomatous sedge forms broad stands with nodding, dark seed spikes. It is wind-pollinated and well suited to tidal marsh structure.
fieldNotes.crowberry: A low evergreen mat with needlelike leaves and shiny black fruit. The tiny flowers are easy to miss, and wind helps carry the pollen.
fieldNotes.lingonberry: Glossy evergreen leaves hug the ground beneath pale bells and red fruit. Bees visit the flowers.
fieldNotes.beachRye: Coarse blue-green blades and tall seed spikes spread through the sand by rhizomes. The grass is wind-pollinated and helps bind dunes.
fieldNotes.bluebunch: A blue-green bunchgrass with upright, often bristly seed spikes. It is wind-pollinated and leaves open ground between clumps.
fieldNotes.switchgrass: An upright clump carries a loose spray of tiny seeds above the leaves. It is wind-pollinated, and the stems add cover into winter.
fieldNotes.pecan: A large canopy tree with divided leaves, hanging spring catkins and nuts. Wind carries the pollen.
fieldNotes.cypress: Feathery needles turn rusty and drop in fall, and mature wet-site trees may develop woody knees. The cones are wind-pollinated.
fieldNotes.aspen: Round leaves flutter on flattened stalks, and pale trunks can form colonies from root shoots. Its catkins are wind-pollinated.
fieldNotes.burOak: A broad shade tree with deeply lobed leaves and acorns in fringed cups. Its catkins shed pollen into the wind.
fieldNotes.westernWheat: Blue-green leaves and narrow spikes rise from spreading underground stems. This wind-pollinated grass can knit bare soil together.
fieldNotes.cottonwood: A fast-growing tree with triangular leaves that flutter in the wind. It is wind-pollinated, and female trees release cottony seeds.
fieldNotes.sandBluestem: Tall blue-green stems with forked seed heads spread through deep sand by rhizomes. Wind pollinates the small flowers.
fieldNotes.saltgrass: Short, stiff blades spread into dense patches on salty soils. The inconspicuous flower spikes are wind-pollinated.
fieldNotes.buffaloGrass: A low gray-green grass spreads by runners into a soft mat. Its small flowers are wind-pollinated.
fieldNotes.sacaton: Large bunches of slender blades carry open sprays of tiny seeds. Wind pollinates the flowers, and the clumps add structure on alkaline ground.
fieldNotes.bigBluestem: Tall stems with three-pronged seed heads turn copper and burgundy in fall. This wind-pollinated grass gives tallgrass plantings their vertical structure.
fieldNotes.postOak: A broad tree with thick leaves whose rounded lobes often form a cross. Its spring catkins are wind-pollinated.
fieldNotes.escarpmentOak: An evergreen oak with a broad, spreading crown and small leathery leaves. Wind carries its pollen, and acorns feed wildlife.
fieldNotes.honeyMesquite: A thorny tree with finely divided leaves, cream flower spikes and long pods. Bees visit the blooms for nectar and pollen.
fieldNotes.idahoFescue: Fine blue-green leaves form tidy bunches with slender seed stalks. It is wind-pollinated and adds soft texture to dry sites.
fieldNotes.bitterbrush: A branching shrub with small, three-lobed leaves and pale yellow spring flowers. Bees visit the fragrant blooms.
fieldNotes.sagebrush: A rounded gray shrub with aromatic, often three-tipped leaves. Its small late-season flowers are chiefly wind-pollinated.
fieldNotes.ricegrass: A fine-leaved bunchgrass carries open seed heads with widely spaced grains. Wind pollinates the flowers, and the seeds provide food for birds.
fieldNotes.fourwing: A gray-green shrub named for the four papery wings on its fruit. Its inconspicuous flowers are wind-pollinated.
fieldNotes.creosote: Glossy paired leaflets and yellow flowers cover an open desert shrub. Native bees, including creosote specialists, visit the blooms.
fieldNotes.blackGrama: Fine leaves and thin seed branches form low patches that spread by runners. Its flowers are wind-pollinated.
fieldNotes.emoryOak: A rounded evergreen to semi-evergreen oak with glossy, often toothed leaves. Its spring flowers are wind-pollinated.
fieldNotes.ohia: A variable shrub or tree with brush-like clusters of stamens, often red. Native nectar-feeding birds and insects use the flowers.
fieldNotes.uluhe: Forking fronds weave into dense mats over moist slopes. This fern reproduces by spores and provides cover without producing pollen or nectar.
fieldNotes.aalii: A branching shrub with narrow leaves and winged seed capsules that can blush pink or red. Its small flowers are mainly wind-pollinated.
fieldNotes.pukiawe: A low or upright shrub with tiny needlelike leaves and white to red fruit. The tiny flowers are easy to overlook beside its berries and fine foliage.
fieldNotes.ohelo: A low shrub with pinkish bell flowers and colorful berries. The blooms offer nectar to flower visitors, and native birds use the fruit.
fieldNotes.naupaka: This fleshy-leaved coastal shrub has white half-fan flowers and pale fruit. Insects visit the flowers, and the dense branching tolerates exposed shores.
fieldNotes.foamflower: Pale flower spires rise above a mound of maple-shaped leaves. Small spring insects visit the blooms, and some forms spread by runners.
fieldNotes.whiteAster: White starry flowers with yellow centers top branching stems in late summer and fall. Bees and flies visit them in partly shaded sites.
fieldNotes.blueAster: Airy sprays of pale blue daisies top stems with heart-shaped lower leaves. Fall flowers draw bees, flies and butterflies.
fieldNotes.cardinalFlower: Tall spikes bear vivid red, two-lipped flowers over a clump of narrow leaves. Hummingbirds are effective visitors to the deep flower tubes.
fieldNotes.beardtongue: Upright stems hold white tubular flowers in loose clusters. Bumblebees and other bees work the open throats.
fieldNotes.crestedIris: Blue to lavender blooms sit low over fans of leaves and show a raised yellow crest. The plant spreads by rhizomes, and bees visit the flowers.
fieldNotes.seaOats: Drooping, flat seed heads hang from arching stems and turn bronze. This wind-pollinated grass can spread by seed in moist shade.
fieldNotes.boneset: Flat sprays of white flowers top stems with paired leaves that join around the stalk. Bees, flies and wasps visit the shallow florets.
fieldNotes.blueVervain: Slender branches carry narrow spikes of purple flowers. Small native bees and other insects work the flowers as they open in rings.
fieldNotes.prairieSmoke: Nodding pink flowers give way to feathery seed plumes that look like smoke. Bumblebees can work their way into the mostly closed flowers.
fieldNotes.roughBlazingStar: Rounded purple tufts climb a tall stem and open from the top down. Bees and butterflies visit the nectar-rich flowers.
fieldNotes.rattlesnakeMaster: Stiff, yucca-like leaves support tall stems of spiky white globes. Bees, wasps and flies visit the many tiny flowers.
fieldNotes.currant: Drooping pink to red flower clusters open on an upright shrub in spring. Hummingbirds and bees use the blooms.
fieldNotes.vineMaple: A small, often multi-stemmed tree with rounded lobed leaves and bright fall color. Small insects visit the spring blossoms before winged seeds form.
fieldNotes.swordFern: Shiny, once-divided fronds arch from an evergreen crown. It reproduces by spores and offers woodland cover without flowers.
fieldNotes.salmonberry: An arching, sometimes prickly shrub with magenta flowers and yellow to red berries. Hummingbirds and bees visit the early blooms.
fieldNotes.blanketflower: Red and yellow daisies rise on upright stems from a low clump. Bees visit the open flower centers.
fieldNotes.blueFlax: Fine upright stems carry pale blue flowers that open and fall quickly. The delicate flowers are visited by small bees.
fieldNotes.rockyPenstemon: Upright stems carry dense blue-violet trumpets over a low rosette. Bumblebees and other bees visit the open tubes.
fieldNotes.junegrass: A low bunchgrass sends up slim stems with compact green to tan seed heads. Wind pollinates the flowers.
fieldNotes.tansyaster: Finely divided leaves set off purple daisies with bright yellow centers. The open flowers attract native bees.
fieldNotes.rockHibiscus: Pale pink to lavender cups open on a low desert perennial with small leaves. Bees visit the flowers.
fieldNotes.antelopeHorns: A low milkweed with greenish flower globes and pods that curve like horns. Many insects visit the flowers, and monarch caterpillars can eat the leaves.
fieldNotes.globemallow: Silvery foliage and apricot-orange cups form a loose desert mound. Bees visit the blooms, including globemallow specialists where they occur.
fieldNotes.calPoppy: Orange to yellow cups stand over fine blue-green leaves. Bees visit for pollen; the flowers close in low light.
fieldNotes.toyon: A large evergreen shrub bears white summer flowers and bright red winter berries. Bees and other small insects visit the flowers.
fieldNotes.deergrass: A large mound of narrow leaves sends slender seed spikes up and outward. It is wind-pollinated and works as a structural bunchgrass.
fieldNotes.alaskaLupine: Blue-purple pea flower spikes stand over palm-shaped leaves. Bumblebees visit the flowers, and the plant can spread by seed.
fieldNotes.nootkaRose: A prickly, spreading shrub carries open pink flowers and large hips. Bees collect pollen from the exposed stamens.
fieldNotes.sitkaSpruce: A tall coastal conifer with sharp needles and hanging cones. Wind carries the pollen; the tree provides wildlife cover.
fieldNotes.bearberry: This trailing evergreen has glossy leaves, pinkish bells and red fruit. Bees visit the spring flowers.
fieldNotes.cloudberry: Low colonies carry single white flowers, with amber fruit on pollinated female plants. Flies and other insects move pollen between flowers.
fieldNotes.labradorTea: A low evergreen shrub with rolled leaf edges, rusty undersides and white flower clusters. Small insects visit the blooms on bog margins.
fieldNotes.koa: A large tree bears curved, blade-like leaf stalks and pale pom-pom flowers. Bees and other insects can visit the flower heads.
fieldNotes.kupukupu: Upright green fronds spread from short runners into a fern groundcover. The fern reproduces by spores and adds shelter without flowers.
fieldNotes.pohuehue: This coastal vine trails over sand with thick leaves and pink-purple morning glory flowers. Bees and other insects can visit the open trumpets.
fieldNotes.iliahi: A woody shrub or small tree with leathery leaves and clusters of small flowers. Its roots tap neighboring plants, so it needs compatible hosts.
fieldNotes.mamane: A shrub or small tree with yellow pea flowers and segmented pods. The flowers provide nectar and the seeds are important food for the palila.
fieldNotes.leadplant: A low, woody prairie plant with silvery divided leaves and dark purple flower spikes. Bees visit the small blossoms.
fieldNotes.dropseed: Fine leaves form fountain-shaped clumps topped by airy seed sprays. The tiny flowers are wind-pollinated.
fieldNotes.blackEyedSusan: Golden rays surround a dark, raised center on upright stems. Bees and other insects visit the flower disks, and birds use the seeds.
fieldNotes.wildGinger: Heart-shaped leaves spread into a low woodland patch. The maroon flowers sit at soil level, where small flies and other insects can reach them.
fieldNotes.goldenAlexanders: Flat clusters of yellow flowers top divided leaves in spring. Small bees and flies visit, and black swallowtail caterpillars can use the foliage.
fieldNotes.seasideGoldenrod: Thick leaves support tall sprays of yellow flowers on coastal sands. Bees and butterflies visit the fall blooms.
fieldNotes.waxMyrtle: A fast-growing evergreen to semi-evergreen shrub with aromatic leaves and waxy fruit. Its small flowers are wind-pollinated, and birds eat the berries.
fieldNotes.dwarfPalmetto: Fan-shaped leaves rise from a usually short or underground trunk. Small insects can visit the pale flower sprays above the foliage.
fieldNotes.blueSage: Blue-violet spikes rise above an upright clump of narrow leaves. Bees visit the tubular flowers.
fieldNotes.autumnSage: An airy subshrub bears tubes that are often red or pink. The blooms draw hummingbirds, and bees also visit.
fieldNotes.blackfootDaisy: Low, spreading mounds carry white daisies with yellow centers. Bees visit the open flowers through the warm season.
fieldNotes.saguaro: A long-lived columnar cactus grows arms as it matures. Its white flowers open at night and are visited by bats, birds and bees.
fieldNotes.desertSage: Silvery leaves form a low mound under violet-blue flower clusters. Native bees visit the blossoms.
fieldNotes.mockOrange: An arching shrub carries fragrant white flowers in early summer. Bees and other insects visit the open blooms.
fieldNotes.westernColumbine: Red and yellow spurred flowers hang above rounded, divided leaves. Hummingbirds and long-tongued bees can reach the nectar.
fieldNotes.insideOutFlower: A low woodland perennial with small white flowers whose petals bend backward. It spreads by rhizomes beneath trees.
fieldNotes.redOsier: This suckering shrub has white flower clusters and bright red young twigs in winter. Bees and flies visit the blooms, and birds use the fruit.
fieldNotes.blackSpruce: A narrow conifer with short needles and small cones that may persist for years. Wind carries pollen from the small male cones.
fieldNotes.dwarfBirch: Low branches carry small, rounded leaves and slender catkins. Wind pollinates the flowers, and the shrub often forms patches in tundra.
fieldNotes.alaskaYarrow: Flat white flower clusters rise above finely divided aromatic foliage. Small bees, flies and wasps visit the shallow flowers.
fieldNotes.naio: A shrub or tree with narrow leaves and small white flowers. Its pale fleshy fruits follow the subtle blooms.
fieldNotes.ulei: This spreading woody shrub has glossy divided leaves and clusters of white flowers. Small insects can visit the open blooms before the pale fruit forms.
fieldNotes.denseBlazingStar: Tall purple spikes open from the top down above narrow leaves. Butterflies and bees visit the clustered florets.
fieldNotes.prairieBlazingStar: An upright wand of shaggy purple flowers rises through narrow foliage. Bees and butterflies feed on the dense bloom.
fieldNotes.mountainMint: Fine mint-scented leaves frame clusters of tiny white flowers. Bees, flower flies and wasps work the open blooms.
fieldNotes.blueLobelia: Blue two-lipped flowers rise on upright stems. Bumblebees visit the flowers, and the plant can reseed in moist open ground.
fieldNotes.zigzagGoldenrod: Broad toothed leaves alternate along angular stems with yellow flower clusters tucked into the leaf axils. The autumn blooms attract bees and flies.
fieldNotes.woodPhlox: Loose clusters of pale blue or lavender flowers rise above low spreading stems. Long-tongued insects, including butterflies, can reach the flowers’ nectar.
fieldNotes.bloodroot: A round lobed leaf unfurls beside a white flower with a golden center. Small spring bees collect pollen from the short-lived flowers.
fieldNotes.jacobsLadder: Pale-blue bells sit above neat rows of leaflets. Native bees visit the spring flowers on this compact woodland perennial.
fieldNotes.blueCohosh: Divided leaves emerge blue-green above inconspicuous yellow-green flowers and later blue seeds. Small bees and flies may visit the flowers.
fieldNotes.joePye: Tall stems with whorled leaves carry broad clusters of dusky pink flowers. Bees and butterflies visit the late summer bloom.
fieldNotes.newEnglandAster: Tall stems carry purple to pink daisies with orange-yellow centers. Fall flowers feed bees and butterflies.
fieldNotes.heathAster: Branching stems hold masses of small white daisies above narrow leaves. Bees and flies visit the autumn flowers.
fieldNotes.sneezeweed: Winged stems hold yellow flowers with raised, dome-shaped centers. The late blooms attract bees and other small insects.
fieldNotes.ironweed: Clusters of deep purple flowers top sturdy, narrow-leaved stems. Butterflies and native bees visit the late summer blooms.
fieldNotes.indianGrass: Tall blue-green leaves turn warm gold beneath plumed seed heads. The grass is wind-pollinated and provides winter cover.
fieldNotes.purpleLoveGrass: Low bunches of leaves send up airy pink-purple clouds of seed heads. It is wind-pollinated and gives late season plantings a soft outline.
fieldNotes.sweetspire: Arching white flower tassels hang from a suckering shrub that often turns red in autumn. Bees and butterflies visit the small flowers.
fieldNotes.fringeTree: White flowers with narrow petals give this small tree a fringed appearance. The spring bloom attracts insects, and female trees can bear dark fruit.
fieldNotes.dwarfFothergilla: This compact shrub bears white bottlebrush flowers before its leaves expand. Bees use the spring bloom, and the leaves often color well in fall.
fieldNotes.greenAndGold: A low mat of hairy leaves carries small yellow daisies. Bees and other insects visit the open flowers.
fieldNotes.spiderwort: Blue three-petaled flowers open above long, arched leaves, often closing by afternoon. Bees collect pollen from the bright anthers.
fieldNotes.blueWildIndigo: A broad clump sends up blue pea-flower spikes that develop dark inflated pods. Bumblebees can open the flowers to reach the nectar.
fieldNotes.virginiaBluebells: Pink buds open into blue bells above soft green leaves. Spring bees visit, and the foliage dies back by summer.
fieldNotes.seaPurslane: Fleshy stems creep along saline ground and carry small pink flowers. The open flowers can be visited by insects.
fieldNotes.saltMarshMallow: An upright perennial bears pink hibiscus-like flowers that open one by one. Bees visit the exposed pollen column.
fieldNotes.tickseed: Golden flowers with toothed ray tips sit above a clump of narrow leaves. Bees visit the flowers, and seedlings can fill nearby gaps.
fieldNotes.purpleConeflower: Drooping pink-purple rays frame a raised coppery cone. Bees and butterflies visit, and the dry heads provide seed for birds.
fieldNotes.beeblossom: White to pink flowers open along tall, airy stems. The long flowering season offers forage to visiting insects.
fieldNotes.plainsConeflower: Yellow or reddish rays hang beneath a tall central cone. Bees visit the raised disks on this upright perennial.
fieldNotes.chocolateFlower: Yellow daisies with darker centers open over a low leafy clump. The chocolate-scented blooms draw bees and other insects.
fieldNotes.texasLantana: An arching shrub carries clusters that shift from yellow to orange and red. Butterflies visit the tubular blooms.
fieldNotes.rockPenstemon: Red tubular flowers rise over a low woody base with narrow leaves. The flower tubes offer nectar to hummingbirds.
fieldNotes.firecracker: Spikes of scarlet tubes rise from tidy basal leaves. Hummingbirds can reach the nectar in the narrow flowers.
fieldNotes.showyGoldeneye: Many small yellow daisies sit on wiry upright stems. Bees and flies work the open disks in late summer.
fieldNotes.silkyLupine: Silvery hairs cover the palm-shaped leaves below blue-purple pea flowers. Bumblebees and other large bees visit the spikes.
fieldNotes.beeplant: An annual with upright stems, pink flowers and long narrow pods. Bees visit the loose flower clusters.
fieldNotes.smoothPenstemon: Blue to purple tubular flowers stand on leafy stems above a basal clump. Bees visit the open-throated flowers.
fieldNotes.rabbitbrush: Gray-green stems hold masses of small yellow fall flowers. Bees, butterflies and flies visit when many other plants have finished blooming.
fieldNotes.ocotillo: Spiny canes leaf out after rain and carry brilliant red flowers at their tips. Hummingbirds visit the bloom.
fieldNotes.scarletBugler: Narrow red tubes rise on straight stems above waxy blue-green leaves. Hummingbirds visit the scarlet flowers.
fieldNotes.narrowleafMilkweed: Narrow leaves line upright stems with pale pink to white flower clusters. Insects visit the flowers and monarch caterpillars feed on the foliage.
fieldNotes.blueEyedGrass: Small blue-violet stars peek above fans of flat, grasslike leaves. Small bees visit the flowers.
fieldNotes.tidytips: This annual has yellow daisies trimmed with crisp white tips. Bees and flies visit the open centers.
fieldNotes.hummingbirdSage: Aromatic leaves spread into patches beneath tall spikes of magenta flowers. Hummingbirds visit the long tubes.
fieldNotes.westernRedbud: This multi-stemmed shrub or small tree bears magenta pea flowers before its rounded leaves open. Early bees visit the flowers.
fieldNotes.redwoodSorrel: Cloverlike leaves form a soft carpet with white to pink-veined flowers. Small insects visit the flowers, and leaves fold under bright light.
fieldNotes.fringecup: Tall spikes of tiny fringed cups rise from a mound of rounded leaves. The flowers turn pinkish with age and can be visited by small insects.
fieldNotes.oceanSpray: Creamy flower sprays hang from arching branches above scalloped leaves. Small bees and flies visit the open flowers.
fieldNotes.pacificBleedingheart: Pink heart-shaped flowers hang above finely divided foliage. Bumblebees visit the spring flowers, and the plant can spread by rhizomes.
fieldNotes.sloughSedge: Dark seed spikes rise above coarse evergreen blades in spreading stands. The sedge is wind-pollinated and adds cover at wet edges.
fieldNotes.redElderberry: Creamy flower clusters open above divided leaves, followed by red fruit. Small bees and flies visit the flowers, and birds use the berries.
fieldNotes.whiteSpruce: Short blue-green needles cover this conical evergreen, which carries slender hanging cones. Wind moves pollen between trees.
fieldNotes.dwarfFireweed: Low leafy stems bear large magenta flowers on gravel bars and disturbed rocky ground. Bees can visit the flowers, and silky seeds travel on the wind.
fieldNotes.tamarack: Soft needles grow in short clusters and turn gold before dropping in autumn. Its small cones are wind-pollinated.
fieldNotes.pohinahina: This coastal shrub spreads low with gray-green leaves and spikes of lavender-blue flowers. Insects visit the flowers.
fieldNotes.akia: A small shrub spreads into a mound with gray-green leaves, tiny yellow flowers and orange-red fruit.
fieldNotes.aweoweo: A branching shrub with pale green leaves and tiny green flower clusters. Wind carries its pollen.
fieldNotes.hapuu: Long, arching fronds rise from a trunk clothed in soft golden fibers. This tree fern reproduces by spores and creates shade and cover.
